correctness.summary: Generic Run<T> reinterprets the element bytes as int/long and sums them with integer arithmetic. For floating-point element types (float has sizeof==4, double has sizeof==8) this adds the raw IEEE-754 bit patterns as integers, producing a meaningless value, and then reinterprets that integer back as the float/double result.
correctness.triggeringInput: float buf[2] = {1.0f, 2.0f}; SuffixSums.Run<float>(buf, 2). Bits 0x3F800000 + 0x40000000 = 0x7F800000 are summed as ints, returning +Infinity instead of 3.0f. Likewise double over {1.0,2.0} gives garbage.
correctness.rootCause: Dispatch is keyed only on sizeof(T)==4/8 and assumes the type is int/long. T:unmanaged also admits float, double, uint, ulong; for float/double the integer addition path is semantically wrong (and for uint/ulong it silently does signed arithmetic on values >Int32/Int64.Max).
correctness.suggestedFix: Do not reinterpret arbitrary unmanaged T as integer for summation. Either constrain to numeric integer types via dedicated typed overloads (as already exist for int/long), or branch on typeof(T)==typeof(float)/typeof(double)/etc. and sum in the correct domain. Remove the sizeof-based int/long reinterpretation for the generic path.

correctness.summary: RangeSum<T> uses the same sizeof(T)==4/8 -> int*/long* reinterpretation as Run<T>, so it sums float/double elements as integer bit patterns, yielding a wrong (or Infinity/NaN) result for floating-point types.
correctness.triggeringInput: double buf[3] = {1.5, 2.5, 3.5}; SuffixSums.RangeSum<double>(buf, 0, 2) reinterprets each double's 64-bit pattern as a long, sums them, and reinterprets back, giving garbage instead of 7.5.
correctness.rootCause: Type dispatch only inspects sizeof(T), not the actual element type, so float/double (and unsigned) elements are summed in the wrong numeric domain via pointer reinterpretation.
correctness.suggestedFix: Branch on the concrete element type (typeof(T)) or provide explicit float/double/uint/ulong overloads, and accumulate in the correct domain instead of reinterpreting bytes as int/long.

perf.summary: Reverse in-place suffix-sum loop is a strict serial dependency chain; reading ptr[i+1] then writing ptr[i] each iteration prevents vectorization and exposes full load-add-store latency per element.
perf.currentCost: len-1 iterations, each with a loop-carried dependency (ptr[i] depends on ptr[i+1] just written). ~1 add + 1 load + 1 store per element on the critical path, no ILP, no SIMD.
perf.proposedChange: Keep the running scalar accumulator out of memory: 'long acc = 0; for (int i = len-1; i >= 0; i--) { acc += ptr[i]; ptr[i] = acc; }'. The accumulator lives in a register, so the store to ptr[i] is no longer a dependency for the next read (next read is ptr[i-1], independent of the store).
perf.rationale: Breaks the memory load->store->load dependency chain into a register accumulator chain (add latency only, ~1 cycle), and removes the dependence of each load on the previous store, letting the CPU overlap loads. Same arithmetic, same in-place result.
perf.risk: None for behavior: produces identical suffix sums and ptr[0] return. Overflow behavior is identical (same unchecked long/int add order).

perf.summary: The sizeof(T)==4 / ==8 branches type-pun via '*(T*)&sum', which forces a stack spill of the accumulator to take its address; a union-free reinterpret avoids the address-taken local.
perf.currentCost: Taking '&sum' marks the accumulator address-exposed, which can inhibit keeping it purely in a register and forces a store/reload at the return; minor but on a hot leaf method.
perf.proposedChange: Return via a typed cast directly: for the 4-byte path 'int r = sum; return *(T*)&r;' is the same; better, since sizeof(T) is a compile-time constant under Burst specialization, the unused branch is dead-code-eliminated already — keep as is, but mark the local with the pattern that avoids re-taking address inside the loop (it already is outside the loop, so impact is low).
perf.rationale: sizeof(T) is constant per Burst monomorphization so the branch folds away; the only residual cost is the address-of on the accumulator at return. Confirming the accumulator is written once after the loop (already true) keeps this near-optimal.
perf.risk: Reinterpret of a 4/8-byte integer to T is only valid when sizeof(T) matches; guarded by the sizeof(T) checks already. No change to semantics.

perf.summary: Naming/contract inconsistency: the typed Run overloads (int*/long*) build an in-place suffix-sum array and return ptr[0]; the generic Run<T> instead computes only the total sum without writing the suffix array, yet Sum<T> returns ptr[0] assuming the suffix array was built. Callers using Run<T> then Sum<T>/RangeSum<T> get inconsistent results.
perf.currentCost: Run<T> does a forward total-sum and never populates the suffix array, so a subsequent Sum<T> (returns ptr[0]) yields the full sum only by coincidence, while RangeSum<T> re-scans O(r-l) instead of using O(1) suffix differences ptr[l]-ptr[r+1].
perf.proposedChange: Make generic Run<T> match the typed overloads: build the in-place suffix sums (acc-accumulator reverse loop), return ptr[0]. Then RangeSum<T> can become O(1): 'ptr[l] - ptr[r+1]' (with ptr[r+1] treated as 0 when r==len-1), instead of an O(n) rescan.
perf.rationale: Aligns the generic with the specialized overloads (consistent observable contract across the class) AND turns RangeSum from O(n) into O(1) once the suffix array exists — an asymptotic win for range queries, which is the entire point of a suffix-sum structure.
perf.risk: This CHANGES observable behavior of Run<T>/RangeSum<T> (Run<T> currently leaves the array untouched). It is a contract fix, not a semantics-preserving micro-opt: only adopt if the intended contract is 'Run builds the suffix array' as the typed overloads imply. RangeSum O(1) form requires the array to be a valid suffix-sum array and bounds r+1<=len.

perf.summary: IComparable<T>.CompareTo is an interface-dispatched call inside the hot loop; for the common blittable numeric types this defeats branchless SIMD min/max and risks a non-devirtualized virtual/interface call.
perf.currentCost: One interface call per element (CompareTo) plus a branch. Even when Burst devirtualizes, CompareTo's three-way result (>0/<0) is heavier than a single compare, and it blocks vectorized min/max.
perf.proposedChange: Provide sizeof(T)-dispatched specializations for the 4-byte and 8-byte integer/float cases (mirroring SuffixSums) using direct '<'/'>' on reinterpreted int/long/float/double, and a branchless select (e.g. min = a + ((b - a) & ((b - a) >> 63)) for longs, or math.min under Burst). Keep the IComparable<T> generic as the fallback.
perf.rationale: Direct relational operators on concrete numeric types are single-cycle, branch-predictable, and SIMD-friendly; Burst auto-vectorizes a running min/max reduction. Removes interface-dispatch overhead and the three-way CompareTo computation on the hot path.
perf.risk: Branchless integer min/max via sign-shift is signed-specific; for unsigned reinterpretation the shift trick is invalid — must dispatch by actual element type, not just sizeof. Float NaN ordering differs between CompareTo and '<', so the float path must preserve the existing CompareTo tie/NaN semantics or be documented as numeric-only.

perf.summary: RangeSum after a suffix-sum build still rescans O(r-l); the structure already supports O(1) range queries via ptr[l]-ptr[r+1].
perf.currentCost: RangeSum is O(r-l+1) per query, defeating the purpose of precomputing suffix sums.
perf.proposedChange: After Run builds the suffix-sum array, expose a RangeSum that returns ptr[l] - (r+1 < len ? ptr[r+1] : 0). This is O(1).
perf.rationale: A suffix-sum (or prefix-sum) array exists precisely to answer range-sum queries in O(1); the current O(n) rescan wastes the precomputation.
perf.risk: Requires ptr to actually hold suffix sums (post-Run) and r+1<=len. The current RangeSum makes no such assumption (it sums raw values), so this is a contract/semantics change, not a drop-in — only valid if RangeSum is defined to operate on a built suffix array.
